data.name: Another Rocket Game
data.detailed_description:
Inspired by and brought to life by the countless hours spent playing one of the old Amiga Classics, "Turboraketti", Another Rocket Game is a game about mastering flying an armed 2D rocket through obstacles and enemies of various kinds.

Apart from the classic split-screen player vs player mode, which was where "Turboraketti" excelled, Another Rocket Game features a complete story based campaign mode, in which you follow Spacey Pete and his trusty rocket Celeste, as they journey to "The Danger Zone" looking for adventure and treasure in the form of "Space Jewels".

Furthermore, all levels can be played and challenged seperately, either by your self, against a computer AI or against friends in split-screen mode.

reviews.review:
Another Rocket Game is a deliberately old-fashioned 2D action game centered on the challenge of controlling a small rocket through dangerous environments where precision, momentum, and quick corrections matter. Developed and published by Games By Nemiz, it takes clear inspiration from classic computer-era rocket games and builds its identity around mechanics rather than elaborate storytelling or modern visual spectacle. The premise is immediately understandable, yet learning to handle the spacecraft confidently gives the experience considerably more depth than its simple presentation might initially suggest.

The campaign follows Spacey Pete and his rocket, Celeste, as they venture into the Danger Zone looking for adventure and valuable Space Jewels. The narrative maintains a playful tone and mainly serves as motivation for moving through the various challenges. This is not a story-heavy adventure filled with lengthy conversations or cinematic sequences. Instead, the emphasis remains firmly on piloting, surviving, fighting, and collecting. That simplicity suits the arcade-inspired structure because the game wastes little time before placing the player behind the controls.

Piloting the rocket is the defining mechanic. Movement requires players to account for direction and thrust rather than expecting the immediate responsiveness associated with conventional platform games. Early attempts can consequently feel awkward, particularly when trying to navigate confined areas or reposition quickly during combat. With practice, however, the unusual handling becomes the game's greatest attraction. Improvement feels connected to the player's growing understanding of momentum and positioning rather than simply acquiring stronger equipment or statistical upgrades.

Combat adds another consideration because maneuvering effectively is only part of the challenge. Players must also deal with opponents while maintaining control of their own spacecraft. Poor positioning can turn an otherwise manageable encounter into a difficult recovery, while accurate movement creates better opportunities to attack. This produces an enjoyable relationship between navigation and combat, where mastering one naturally improves performance in the other. The difficulty can occasionally feel unforgiving, but that is consistent with the retro philosophy behind the overall design.

The campaign is complemented by the ability to tackle levels individually, which is useful for practicing troublesome sections or attempting stronger performances. Computer-controlled opponents provide competition when playing alone, while local split-screen multiplayer introduces a more unpredictable dimension. Competing against another player makes the physics-oriented movement especially entertaining because both participants are simultaneously trying to control their rockets and react to each other's decisions. It is a particularly suitable setup for players who enjoy compact competitive games that can be understood quickly but take considerably longer to master.

Replayability also comes from score chasing. Online high-score functionality encourages players to revisit completed stages and improve their results instead of treating successful completion as the absolute endpoint. This fits the mechanics particularly well. Once a player becomes comfortable with the rocket, previously difficult sections can be approached more efficiently, creating a noticeable sense of personal improvement. Steam achievements provide additional objectives, while Remote Play Together gives the local multiplayer component greater flexibility when playing with friends.

Visually, Another Rocket Game embraces simplicity. Its 2D presentation prioritizes clarity over graphical detail, resulting in an aesthetic that feels much closer to an independent interpretation of an older computer game than a contemporary action production. That approach will not appeal equally to everyone. Players looking for sophisticated animation, cinematic effects, or highly detailed environments may find it visually sparse. For its intended style, however, the straightforward graphics keep attention focused on movement, enemies, hazards, and the immediate action.

Music contributes considerably to the game's personality. The soundtrack features melodies composed by Mr.Lou and supports the energetic, nostalgic character of the gameplay. This becomes especially important during repeated attempts because mastering levels often means experiencing the same environments multiple times. An enjoyable soundtrack makes that repetition easier to appreciate and helps give the otherwise minimalist presentation additional character.

The game's limitations largely come from the same focused design that gives it charm. Players who want extensive progression systems, elaborate storytelling, large amounts of exploration, or constant mechanical variety may consider the package too modest. Its lasting appeal depends heavily on whether the player enjoys improving through repetition, mastering unconventional movement, chasing scores, and competing against other players. The controls may also discourage anyone unwilling to spend time learning how the rocket behaves.

Steam Deck compatibility should be approached with some caution. The game does not have an official Valve Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification. Its lightweight 2D presentation is unlikely to be demanding from a hardware perspective, and the gameplay concept is naturally appropriate for handheld controls, but the absence of an official compatibility rating means a completely trouble-free experience cannot be guaranteed. Steam Deck owners may need to rely on Proton and could potentially encounter control, interface, display, or configuration issues. It is therefore better regarded as an unverified Steam Deck title rather than one with confirmed full support.

Another Rocket Game works best for players who appreciate compact arcade experiences where mechanical mastery is more important than spectacle. Its combination of momentum-based rocket handling, combat, individual challenges, score competition, campaign progression, and multiplayer creates a surprisingly complete framework around a simple central idea. It remains unmistakably niche, but there is satisfaction in progressing from struggling with basic movement to confidently maneuvering through hazards and opponents.

For retro-action enthusiasts and players attracted to unusual physics-oriented controls, this is an interesting independent game with enough challenge and replay value to justify repeated sessions. Its modest production values and specialized gameplay prevent it from being universally appealing, but its commitment to its central concept gives it personality. Rather than attempting to offer dozens of unrelated features, it concentrates on making rocket control itself the challenge, and that focused approach is ultimately its strongest quality.

Rating: 6/10
